name: Mitochondrial Disorder Due to a Defect in Mitochondrial Protein Synthesis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Mitochondrial Protein Synthesis Defect Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Presence of multisystemic clinical features including neurological and muscular symptoms
Biochemical evidence of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex deficiencies in muscle or fibroblasts
Identification of pathogenic variants in nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial translation machinery components
Muscle biopsy showing ragged-red fibers or cytochrome c oxidase (COX) deficient fibers
Elevated blood or CSF lactate levels indicating mitochondrial dysfunction

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria (clinical features, biochemical evidence, and genetic confirmation) must be met for definitive diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Muscle biopsy and lactate levels support diagnosis but are not mandatory if genetic confirmation is obtained.

searchTerms: muscle biopsy showing ragged red fibers
abnormal muscle fibers with red staining
very high lactic acid in blood

occasional.notes: Poor growth in infancy or childhood

laboratory: Elevated blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate
Deficient activities of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes I, III, IV, and/or V
Elevated serum creatine kinase in some cases
imaging: Brain MRI showing basal ganglia abnormalities and cerebral atrophy
Muscle MRI may show fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy
genetic: Pathogenic variants in nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial translation factors (e.g., TSFM, MRPS16, GFM1)
Mitochondrial DNA depletion or multiple deletions secondary to nuclear gene defects
other: Muscle biopsy demonstrating ragged-red fibers and COX-negative fibers
Electron microscopy showing abnormal mitochondrial morphology

distinguishingFeatures: Primary mitochondrial DNA depletion without direct translation machinery defects
Often presents with severe infantile hepatopathy or myopathy
Characteristic symmetrical lesions in basal ganglia and brainstem on MRI
Usually caused by mutations in mitochondrial or nuclear genes affecting respiratory chain

redFlags: Rapidly progressive external ophthalmoplegia in infancy or early childhood
Severe lactic acidosis refractory to standard treatment
Multisystem involvement with neurological deterioration and muscle weakness
references: Gorman GS, Schaefer AM, Ng Y, et al. Mitochondrial diseases. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2016;2:16080.
Smeitink J, van den Heuvel L, DiMauro S. Mitochondrial medicine: a metabolic perspective on the pathology of oxidative phosphorylation disorders. Cell Metab. 2001;3(4):289-296.
Antonicka H, Sasarman F, Nishimura T, et al. Mutations in mitochondrial translation elongation factor G1 cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency. Nat Genet. 2006;38(11): 124-129.
